newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Unions launch mass Europe for Jobs campaign.
newsitem.headline: Unions launch mass Europe for Jobs campaign.

text.p: Thousands of Europeans are expected to take part this month in an international cycle race and mass rallies to demand more European Union action to fight unemployment and increasingly precarious working conditions.

The events, organised by the European Trade Union Confederation, are designed to urge EU leaders to write strong social and employment policies into a revised EU treaty due to be agreed at a summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17.
"The moment has come to rebalance Europe," ETUC secretary general Emilio Gabaglio told a news conference.
People wanted the 15-member EU bloc to be more than a single market and a single currency, he said.
They wanted a Union which responded to their needs, and that included work for the 20 million EU citizens who do not have jobs and proper protection and rights for people who do.

The ETUC's Europe for Jobs campaign kicks off on May 13 when 1996 Tour de France winner Bjarne Riis sets off from Metz in France at the head of a five-day cycle race to Brussels via Luxembourg, Germany and the Dutch town of Maastricht, where EU leaders agreed in 1992 to create an Economic and Monetary Union.

The campaign culminates on May 28 in a European Day of Action for Employment in 25 European countries, marked by rock concerts, public information campaigns and union representations to prime ministers and EU officials in Brussels.

Gabaglio said the ETUC was pleased EU member states were considering giving the EU more explicit powers to set employment and social policy and that Britain's new Labour government had promised to sign up to the EU's Social Chapter.
But the trade unions still thought the proposed reforms to the EU treaty were too weak.
They wanted EU leaders to give the Union a stronger mandate to fight unemployment and allow more laws on workers' rights to be decided by a qualified majority rather than unanimity, Gabaglio said.

The unions were also disappointed that the EU states were not even considering including basic trade union rights in the new EU treaty, when the much-criticised snap decision by car maker Renault to close its plant at Vilvoorde, Belgium, had demonstrated how important these rights were, he said.
"Companies are becoming international. We need workers' rights to be recognised at the same level," he said.
